title: Security Operations Best Practices
summary: Baseline controls for identity, logging, network, endpoint and data.
content:
# Security Operations Best Practices

## Identity and access
Enforce least privilege: an account should hold only the rights its role requires, and
administrative rights should be separate accounts rather than an attribute of a daily-use
one. Require multi-factor authentication for all remote access, all administrative access and
all access to sensitive data. Review access quarterly and remove what is no longer needed;
accumulated permissions are how a minor compromise becomes a major one.

Service accounts need particular care. Give each one a single purpose, deny it interactive
logon, rotate its credentials on a schedule, and record where its keys are deployed so
rotation is possible in practice rather than only in policy.

## Logging and monitoring
Centralise logs off the systems that generate them - an attacker with host access will clear
local logs. Retain long enough to investigate a breach discovered late; ninety days is a
common floor and a year is safer. Synchronise clocks across the estate, because a timeline
assembled from unsynchronised sources is not a timeline.

Log authentication (success and failure), privilege changes, configuration changes, and access
to sensitive data. Monitor that logging itself is still flowing: a source that goes quiet is an
alert, not an absence of alerts.

## Network
Segment the network so that compromise of one host does not grant reach across the estate.
Deny egress by default and allow only what is required; most exfiltration and command-and-
control depends on unrestricted outbound access. Do not expose management interfaces to the
internet. Inspect and log traffic at segment boundaries.

## Endpoint and patching
Deploy endpoint detection and response broadly, and alert on tampering with it. Patch on a
risk-based schedule with an emergency path for actively exploited vulnerabilities. Maintain
an accurate asset inventory; you cannot patch or monitor what you do not know you have.

## Data
Classify data and apply controls proportionate to classification. Encrypt sensitive data at
rest and in transit. Minimise what is collected and retained - data you do not hold cannot be
breached.

## Resilience
Back up to storage the production environment cannot reach or delete, and test restoration
regularly. An untested backup is an assumption. Exercise the incident response plan at least
annually, including the communication paths, which are usually what fail first.
